note: Opening IDEAS §1.4 (seal staleness and quorum), the last §1 entry with work in front of it. The session's finding is that §1.4 is two questions in one entry and they are in very different states: staleness is built, and quorum is blocked on a fact about the world rather than on code. Two of §1.4's own claims turned out to be stale, both in the direction its author was not looking. Every row is a draft proposal for a human to weigh at `nestor ui`, not a taken decision. Checked by running, not by reading: scripts/count_countersignatures.py and scripts/due_for_reverification.py against ~/github/willow-memory/.willow/nestor/nestor.db.ledger.jsonl (21 entries, chain verifies, read-only).

decisions.question: IDEAS §1.4 says 'a quorum is still not recorded at all (§6.26)'. Is that true?
decisions.commitment: No — false since 2026-08-06, when §6.26 shipped and a concurring verifier began writing a `countersign` entry. The entry is corrected in place rather than rewritten, in the same shape as its 2026-08-06 correction, so both driftings stay visible.
decisions.why: This premise had already been corrected once — the original entry claimed 'the data is there' and it was not — and then went stale again in the opposite direction: the data IS there now and the entry still says it is not. An entry that is argued rather than checked drifts on whichever side its author was not looking at, and this one has now demonstrated that twice. Worth recording as a pattern and not just a typo.

decisions.question: Step 2 of the quorum memo — does anyone countersign? — has never been run against a deployment. Can it be run here?
decisions.commitment: Yes, and it was. The Nestor instance exposed over MCP keeps a real chain outside this checkout (21 entries, 11 seals, chain verifies). The verdict is `no second reviewer`: one named actor in the whole chain, so its zero is evidence that nobody was asked, not that reviewers decline to concur.
decisions.why: §6.42 said the tool was blocked on a real chain and named the checkout's absence of one. It is not the only chain on the machine. The run is read-only — no store, no matcher, no writes — and the tool refuses to count over a chain that does not verify, so pointing it at a live ledger cannot disturb or misreport it. The result is a better blocker than the one it replaces: step 2 is now run-and-inconclusive-for-a-stated-reason rather than unrun.

decisions.question: Does that verdict license designing N-of-M?
decisions.commitment: No. The question moves from 'does anyone countersign?' to 'is there a chain anywhere with two reviewers in it?', and on this machine today there is not. N-of-M stays unbuilt.
decisions.why: The memo's rule is that N-of-M is a schema change to the audited path and designing one for users who have not been shown to exist is how a field ends up carrying a distinction nothing else makes. A zero from a single-reviewer chain is exactly the evidence that rule was written to refuse. Building it now because the measurement finally ran would be treating 'I looked' as 'I found', which is the same conflation the tool itself is built to prevent.

decisions.question: §1.4's first suggestion is 'seal age surfaced in provenance', and §6.10 is titled 'Seal age in provenance (display only) — shipped'. Was it shipped?
decisions.commitment: In the browser only. §6.10's body is about `nestor ui`'s memory-list chips; `answer.provenance` carried who sealed a row and never when. Shipped now: `Curator.get` gains `seal_age` — `{days, last, verifier, kind, uncorroborated_tail}` — for sealed rows, read from the chain, display only, with no key at all on a draft.
decisions.why: The entry title said provenance and its body said chips, so for three months the map read as though §1.4's first bullet was covered. The auditor months later and the model calling `nestor_provenance` are the two readers §1.4 names, and neither could see the age. Reading it from the ledger rather than a column is the memo's own conclusion: a stored age is unsigned mutable state beside the data it governs — `weight` is written by every seal path and absent from `signing._message`, so anyone with write access could reset a decayed value while every signature still verified.

decisions.question: What does the age report when the pair's freshest decision is the chain's last line?
decisions.commitment: It says so: `uncorroborated_tail: true`. The field is carried rather than dropped, and named for what it means rather than for the `tail` flag it comes from.
decisions.why: The last line of a hash chain is the one line the chain does not vouch for (IDEAS §5.5). An age resting on it is an age nothing corroborates, and an audit view that knows that and stays quiet is the silence this repository keeps turning into a sentence. It cost one boolean to say.

decisions.question: Where does 'what counts as a freshening decision' live, now that three callers need it?
decisions.commitment: In `nestor.staleness.FRESHENING`, read by the UI queue, the CLI listing and `Curator.get` alike. Not restated in the curator.
decisions.why: A countersignature resets the clock because it is a second person deciding the row is good now. That rule in three copies is three chances to disagree about whether a re-verification counts — and the repository has fixed that exact shape four times (the secret-scan list, the dep-audit invocation, the lint pins, and the seal-vs-import refusal set). One definition, three readers.
